description: We are Te Falta Tech, five people in Madrid tackling Challenge 04. We build Metis, an AI companion for every astronaut that works offline and is fully voice-controlled. It watches their vital signs, spots problems early, alerts the crew and guides them step by step through emergencies, when Earth is too far to answer fast. We combine AI, software, research, legal and business. We care about technology that looks after real people. Join us and help Metis save a life 400 km above Earth.
summary: Metis is a private, offline AI health companion for astronauts. It builds each person's own baseline (vitals, sleep, mood) and compares it with the cabin environment. When something drifts it warns the astronaut first, and the crew if there is no answer. Metis stays with you throughout the mission: now and then it checks in to ask how you are doing and, when needed, how you are feeling, without ever overwhelming you. In an emergency it guides the crew step by step with a deterministic triage tree whose steps cite published sources, and it prepares a summary for the flight surgeon. Everything runs locally, because on a Mars mission a call to Earth can take up to 20 minutes each way and the medical officer may be the one who collapses.
details:
What it does and how it works

Metis is a private, offline AI health companion that stays with each crew member during a long-duration mission. Our demo scenario is a fictional crew on the way to Mars. It does five things:

1. Personal baseline. It learns what is normal for each person (heart rate, sleep, mood) and flags drift against that baseline, not against a population average.

2. Sleep and cabin air. It compares sleep with cabin CO2 (NASA limits the one-hour average to 3 mmHg, NASA-STD-3001) and tells the astronaut when short nights line up with CO2 peaks.

3. Always there, never intrusive. Metis talks to you now and then to ask how you are doing. A short daily check-in tracks mood and fatigue, and a validated four-question screen (PHQ-4) runs every two weeks. It adapts its advice to your answers and offers a talk with the medical officer or a psychologist when needed, without overwhelming you.

4. Guided triage and emergencies. A deterministic decision tree whose steps cite published sources guides the crew through chest pain, a collapsed crewmate (CPR in microgravity), mental-health concerns and fatigue. The language model only phrases the words. It never decides the medical step.

5. Crew console and Earth link. A console shows the crew, alerts and the medical kit. In an emergency Metis messages the flight surgeon and tells the crew it has done so. The Earth view shows what arrives after the light-time delay, with a store-and-forward queue when there is no link. Each role sees only what it should.

It is hands-free: saying "Metis" starts a conversation, and emergencies need no wake word.

Benefits and intended impact

Early warnings tuned to the person. Care that keeps working when Earth cannot answer in time (up to 20 minutes each way on a Mars mission). Privacy by design: no cloud and one Metis per astronaut. Support for the whole crew, including the Crew Medical Officer, who can also become a patient. Our goal is a trustworthy, explainable first layer of care that hands a compact summary to the flight surgeon and fails safely.

How it is creative

Metis is a companion, not a dashboard. It compares you with yourself, it links body and habitat (sleep with CO2), it talks with you instead of waiting for you to check a screen, and it is designed for a small bone-conduction module worn behind the ear.

Factors we considered

Communication delay and blackouts, so everything runs offline. Safety, so the medical logic is rule-based with cited sources and there is a scripted fallback if the AI is unavailable. Privacy and roles. Crew workload, so check-ins are short and spaced out. Honesty about limits.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Python 3.12 (FastAPI) and TypeScript/React (Vite) with three.js for a 3D body model. A local AI runs on the habitat computer: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 via llama.cpp, Kokoro-82M for speech and whisper.cpp for recognition. It runs on ordinary laptops with no GPU, and 366 automated tests pass. The video was made with HTML/CSS/JS scenes, headless Chrome and FFmpeg. The earpiece render was made in Blender.
